title: IEnumerable versus IQueryable (delegates vs expression trees)
hook: The lambda looks the same in both cases. On IEnumerable it is a Func delegate the Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler runs in your process. On IQueryable it is an expression tree a provider must translate — or throw.

blocks.text: IEnumerable<T> and IQueryable<T> both let you write LINQ queries, but they compile lambdas differently. Enumerable.Where takes Func<T, bool> — a compiled delegate that runs in your process. Queryable.Where takes Expression<Func<T, bool>> — an immutable tree of nodes (method calls, constants, binary operations) that a provider walks and may rewrite to SQL, a search DSL, or another remote language. The C# compiler picks the overload from the source type. An expression tree is not executable code; it is data describing what you want.

entries.plainDefinition: A sequence you enumerate in process. LINQ operators take Func delegates and run locally.
A queryable sequence backed by an IQueryProvider. LINQ operators build expression trees the provider may translate.
An immutable data structure representing code as a tree of nodes, not compiled IL.
The engine that executes or translates an IQueryable expression tree.
entries.example: Entity Framework Core's provider translates trees to SQL.

blocks.text: Confusing IEnumerable and IQueryable is how in-memory code "worked on a list" and then timed out on a database table. AsQueryable() on a List<T> still executes locally — it is not a database. ToList() or AsEnumerable() in the middle of a remote chain is the wall: everything after runs as LINQ to Objects on pulled data. Custom instance methods in a Where are fine on IEnumerable and usually fatal on a provider. Statement lambdas, await, local functions, and many newer C# features cannot go into expression trees.

blocks.title: Interview-level scope
blocks.body: Know the interface split and the tree limits. You do not need Entity Framework Core mapping details in this language track — just understand that a provider translates a subset of C#.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Write the same lambda

items.title: Compiler picks the overload
items.body: IEnumerable source → Func delegate. IQueryable source → Expression<Func<...>> tree.

items.title: IEnumerable executes locally
items.body: The JIT compiles the Func and runs it for each element in the process.

items.title: IQueryable defers to the provider
items.body: The provider walks the expression tree and may translate it to SQL or throw if it cannot.

snippet.label: Same lambda, two compile-time types
snippet.explanation: AsQueryable on a List still executes locally after compiling the tree. Writing Expression<Func<...>> forces a tree you can inspect or Compile() back to a Func.

snippet.label: AsEnumerable as the in-process boundary
snippet.explanation: AsEnumerable switches overload resolution to Enumerable. The first Where may still run in the provider. CustomScoreCurve never has to be translatable.

snippet.label: ToList is a materialization wall
snippet.explanation: ToList executes the remote query and stores results. Everything after runs as LINQ to Objects on the in-memory list.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Believing AsQueryable() sends a List to SQL. Putting a statement lambda or local function in a provider Where. Turning this topic into an Entity Framework Core lecture — out of scope for this track. Forgetting that ToList in the middle of a remote chain pulls all matching rows into memory.

blocks.text: IEnumerable LINQ compiles lambdas to **Func** delegates and runs **LINQ to Objects** in-process — each operator adds iterator allocations. IQueryable compiles to **Expression** trees for a provider; translation limits are the interview focus, not EF mapping details. AsQueryable() on List<T> still executes locally after building a thin expression wrapper. ToList() and AsEnumerable() are **materialization walls**: everything after runs as Func-based LINQ to Objects on pulled data. Expression trees cannot contain statement bodies, await, or most local functions — custom instance methods in Where usually fail translation. On in-memory chains after materialization, **TryGetNonEnumeratedCount** helps avoid double enumeration; **PLINQ** (AsParallel) is a separate pointer for CPU-bound partitioning, not a provider feature. How to prove it in production: log provider SQL versus client-side filter ratio; catch NotSupportedException from untranslatable predicates before deploy.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Provider may translate; subset of C#

snippet.label: Expression tree limits versus IEnumerable freedom
snippet.explanation: The wall pattern is the senior interview answer: translatable predicates on IQueryable, then ToList, then full C# Func LINQ to Objects with iterator cost accepted on the smaller set.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying AsQueryable on List sends work to SQL — it does not. Turning the answer into an EF Core lecture instead of Func versus Expression. Putting custom methods in IQueryable Where and blaming the provider at runtime. Strong answer: IEnumerable Func in-process; IQueryable Expression for provider; ToList wall; PLINQ is separate in-memory opt-in.

interviewTakeaways: IEnumerable: Func delegates, LINQ to Objects in-process with iterator allocations per operator.
IQueryable: Expression trees plus provider translation — subset of C# in predicates.
ToList/AsEnumerable is the materialization wall; after it, full C# Func LINQ runs locally.

60s: IEnumerable compiles to Func and runs here. IQueryable builds Expression trees for a provider. AsQueryable on List is still local. ToList is the wall. PLINQ AsParallel is in-memory CPU opt-in, not remote translation.
Follow-up: why does a local function in IQueryable Where fail?
commonPitfalls: Believing AsQueryable sends a List to SQL — rejected; it wraps Enumerable with expression nodes then runs locally.
Strong answer: only true IQueryable from a provider translates; List.AsQueryable is still in-process.
Putting a statement lambda or local function in a provider Where — expression trees reject most statement bodies.
Turning this into an EF Core mapping session — out of scope; know Func vs Expression and the wall.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS passes functions. There is no compiler-built AST for array.filter that a SQL engine consumes. ORMs in Node parse functions as strings or use a DSL. C# uniquely has Expression<T> in the language.
Prisma/Knex build query DSLs like IQueryable expression trees. Array.filter is always Func-like in-memory execution — no translation wall unless you use an ORM.
